# The checkout tests went green the week we fixed the keyboard problem and I do not trust it

## Problem Description

`com.northwind.shop`, Android, Kotlin. For most of this year the five checkout
instrumentation tests were red about half the time. The symptom was always the
same shape: a tap that should have landed on a button landed on the soft
keyboard instead, and the next assertion blew up with nothing matching.

Tomas spent the last sprint on it. Since build 4620 all five pass on every run
and the job time dropped from eleven minutes to seven. Miriam wants to use that
to retire the manual checkout regression pass before the 19 September release -
it is forty minutes of somebody's Friday and she has wanted it gone since June.

What is nagging me is that two checkout bugs reached customers in the August
release while this job was green, and one of them was in an area I am fairly
sure these tests cover. I asked Tomas to write down what he changed, per test,
and he did; it is attached along with the current test class, the run log from
4620, the log from 4611 (that was the afternoon the staging backend was in
pieces and we ran the job against it anyway), the cart adapter, and the note
from the August manual pass.

Go through it and tell me whether the green means what Miriam thinks it means.
Then fix whatever needs fixing - I would rather have a slower job that tells me
the truth than a fast one that does not.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `app/src/androidTest/java/com/northwind/shop/CheckoutTest.kt` wherever
   your findings call for it. Do not reduce the number of `@Test` methods, and
   do not change `CheckoutActivity`'s ids or layout.
2. Write `docs/checkout-suite-review.md`: take the five tests one at a time,
   say what Tomas changed, say whether that test's green is worth anything, and
   say what you did.
3. Give Miriam a straight answer about the manual regression pass in the same
   document.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `app/src/androidTest/java/com/northwind/shop/CheckoutTest.kt` wherever
   your findings call for it. Do not reduce the number of `@Test` methods, and
   do not change `CheckoutActivity`'s ids or layout.
2. Write `docs/checkout-suite-review.md`: take the five tests one at a time,
   say what Tomas changed, say whether that test's green is worth anything, and
   say what you did.
3. Give Miriam a straight answer about the manual regression pass in the same
   document.
assertions: The answer identifies that `removingAnItemUpdatesTheCart` passes regardless of whether the removal happened, and replaces the final check with an assertion that cannot pass while the line is still in the cart - the always-attached header (`R.id.cart_subtotal` / `R.id.cart_line_count`), or the adapter's item count - not a presence check on a row. Leaving the `doesNotExist()` assertion in place, or reporting the test as trustworthy, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the mechanism as well as the fix: the title is line 9 of 12 with four rows visible and `CartAdapter.refresh` scrolls back to position 0, so the view is detached either way, corroborated by the test passing on build 4611 where every remove call returned 500. Noticing only that 4611 passed, without explaining why the matcher cannot see the row, scores at most half.

`expiredPromoCodeIsRejected` is changed so that it fails when an expired code is accepted - asserting the refusal message, or the absence of a discount on the total, rather than `isDisplayed()` on `R.id.promo_error_container`. Full marks require naming the evidence: 4611 raised the same container for every code submitted, and NW-2244 shipped with the container on screen and the discount applied. Restoring the exact copy string with no acknowledgement of Tomas's reason for removing it scores at most half. Leaving the container check as the assertion scores zero.

Miriam gets an explicit yes or no, tied to what the suite actually covers once the weakened assertions are repaired, and to the fact that the one August defect the automation nominally covered was found manually rather than by the job. An answer that leaves the decision implicit, or that clears the pass for retirement on the strength of 21 consecutive green runs, scores zero.

The `Thread.sleep(2000)` in `placeOrderButtonIsReachableOnASmallScreen` is removed and the underlying reachability handled by a mechanism the framework can synchronise on. Keeping the sleep, or moving it to a helper, scores zero. Replacing it with a polling loop or a longer sleep also scores zero.

`deliveryDateAppearsAfterAddressEntry` is either restored to the run or explicitly carried as a named, dated, owned gap in `docs/checkout-suite-review.md` - and the review states that the checkout suite has been reporting green with this coverage switched off since the keyboard work. Deleting the test scores zero. Leaving `@Ignore` untouched and unmentioned scores zero.

`emailFieldAcceptsPlusAddressing` is left as it is. Its fix was the right one and build 4611 shows it passing for a reason unrelated to the backend. Rewriting it, restructuring it, or reporting it as suspect alongside the other two scores zero here.
`docs/checkout-suite-review.md` exists and covers all five tests individually. A document that discusses the suite in aggregate without a per-test verdict scores at most half.

# The German lane has been red since the day we added it and the English one never has

## Problem Description

`com.northwind.shop`, Android, Kotlin. We open in Germany on 6 October. Three
weeks ago we added a second instrumentation lane so the German build gets the
same nightly coverage the English one has had for two years.

The English lane is 9 for 9 every night. The German lane has failed the same
five tests every night since it was created and has never once been green.
Nobody has had time to look properly because we have all been on launch work.

Miriam's view is that the lane is the problem: "we threw it together in an
afternoon, the selectors in it are brittle, put ids on everything and let's move
on." Hendrik wants to switch the lane off until after launch on the grounds that
a job nobody trusts is worse than no job. The freeze is Friday and I have to
tell them something on Thursday morning.

Attached: the German test class, the two string files, the price formatter and
the application class, the in-app language setting, the CI workflow that launches
both lanes, and the nightly logs from the 8th and the 11th - the class order
differs between those two nights because we added a shard.

Work out what is actually happening and put the lane in a state where its result
means something. I would rather be told the lane cannot tell us what we hoped
than be handed a green one.

## Output Specification

1. Change whatever needs changing in the supplied files. Keep all nine `@Test`
   methods in `SignupFlowDeTest` and do not delete the lane.
2. Write `docs/de-lane-findings.md`: go through the nine tests, say what each
   one's current result is worth, and say what you changed.
3. In the same document, say what you are telling Miriam and Hendrik on
   Thursday, including anything the lane will still not be covering on Friday.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change whatever needs changing in the supplied files. Keep all nine `@Test`
   methods in `SignupFlowDeTest` and do not delete the lane.
2. Write `docs/de-lane-findings.md`: go through the nine tests, say what each
   one's current result is worth, and say what you changed.
3. In the same document, say what you are telling Miriam and Hendrik on
   Thursday, including anything the lane will still not be covering on Friday.
assertions: The answer establishes that `Locale.setDefault(Locale.GERMANY)` in `@Before` does not put the app into German - the activity's resources resolve from the device configuration, which the workflow leaves at the AVD default, and the rule has already created the activity before `@Before` runs - and applies the locale where resource resolution actually sees it, before the activity under test is created (device/app locale, or the app's own locale API, driven per lane). Any answer whose fix is to swap the failing text matchers for ids, source the expectations from `getString`, or otherwise make the five failures stop while nothing changes about the language the app renders in, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the diagnosis as well as the change: the lane has been comparing German expectations against an English app for three weeks, so its red is not a German finding. Identifying that the app is rendering English without changing how the locale is applied scores at most half.

MUST NOT make `cartTotalIsFormattedForTheLocale` pass by editing its expected string, accepting either format, or asserting on the label instead of the amount. Doing so scores zero. Full marks require naming the cause - `PriceFormatter` holds one `NumberFormat` built from whatever `Locale.getDefault()` was when the object initialised, and `NorthwindApp.onCreate` forces that to happen at process start - and stating the user-visible consequence, that a customer switching language through `LanguageSettings` gets German text with the old number format. Reporting it as a defect without connecting it to the in-app language switch scores at most half.

`germanTranslationsAreLoaded` is called out as unable to fail: it asserts the heading equals `context.getString(R.string.signup_heading)`, comparing the app to itself, so it passes in every locale including the English one the lane has actually been running. Full marks require it to be changed into something that can fail. Counting it among the four honest passes, or leaving it untouched and unmentioned, scores zero.

The answer connects the 2026-09-09 failures in `ReceiptTest` and `SearchTest` - German date and thousands separators in classes that have nothing to do with the German lane - to the process-wide default this class sets and never restores, notes that all of it happened under one pid, and fixes it both at the source (restore the previous default after each test) and structurally (per-test process isolation in `app/build.gradle`). Attributing those two failures to flake, to the shard split, or to the German app build scores zero. Fixing only one of the two levels scores at most half.

The `onView(withText("Weiter"))` in `continueButtonAdvancesToDelivery` is replaced with a match on the button's id or content description. Leaving it, or replacing it with the English label, scores zero.

Miriam and Hendrik get an explicit position on the freeze: what the lane will genuinely cover on Friday, what it will not, and whether the German launch is exposed. Recommending the lane be switched off scores zero. A report that stops at the technical findings without a recommendation scores at most half.
`docs/de-lane-findings.md` exists and gives a per-test verdict for all nine tests. A document that treats the five failures as one item scores at most half.

# Nineteen tests are red in the nightly and every one of them passes on its own

## Problem Description

`com.northwind.shop`, Android, Kotlin. Twenty-three instrumentation tests across
four classes. Since 3 September the nightly has been red on nineteen of them.
Karim has been through the list one test at a time on the same emulator image
and every single one passes when he runs it by itself, in nine seconds or less.
Run the whole thing and it takes twenty-two minutes and comes back with nineteen
failures.

There are three theories on the table and I do not have a way to choose between
them.

Rosa wants to pin the execution order. Her argument is that the nightly on the
8th had a different order and a different set of failures, so order is clearly
the variable, and that we should lock in the alphabetical order and move on. She
also says state cannot be the problem because she turned per-test isolation on
back in March and it has been in the build file ever since.

Karim wants to raise the idle timeout to a hundred and twenty seconds. His
argument is that every failure is a timeout, the emulator is slow, and twenty-six
seconds was always a guess.

Tomas thinks it is the onboarding flag. `AccountTest` writes a preference that
the home screen reads, and he has watched it change behaviour on a later screen
by hand.

Attached: the two classes that matter, the idling class, the cart repository and
activity, the module build file, the nightly logs from the 11th and the 8th,
Karim's single-test runs, and the staging gateway log for the 11th.

Work out what is actually leaking, fix it, and tell me which of the three
proposals survives.

## Output Specification

1. Make the full nightly report what the single-test runs report. Keep all
   twenty-three `@Test` methods and do not change what any test asserts.
2. You may change production code under `app/src/main/` and the module build
   file.
3. Write `docs/nightly-isolation.md`: what is leaking between tests, why a test
   run on its own does not see it, and a verdict on each of the three proposals
   with the reason it does or does not hold.
evals.expected_output:
1. Make the full nightly report what the single-test runs report. Keep all
   twenty-three `@Test` methods and do not change what any test asserts.
2. You may change production code under `app/src/main/` and the module build
   file.
3. Write `docs/nightly-isolation.md`: what is leaking between tests, why a test
   run on its own does not see it, and a verdict on each of the three proposals
   with the reason it does or does not hold.
assertions: The answer establishes that the `clearPackageData` runner argument has no effect on its own - the orchestrator has to be selected in `testOptions` and its artifact present - cites the evidence that nothing is isolated today (one pid across all twenty-three tests in both nightly logs), and turns real per-test isolation on in `app/build.gradle`. Repeating Rosa's claim that isolation has been on since March, or leaving `app/build.gradle` unchanged, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Enabling the orchestrator without noticing that the existing argument was inert, or without citing the shared pid, scores at most half.

Full marks require all three of: the registration in `CartTest.@Before` is never undone, so a process-wide resource stays registered for every later class; `CartRepository.syncPendingChanges` decrements only in `onResponse`, so the 503 on `POST /v1/cart/sync` leaves the counter above zero permanently; and the fix covers both - decrement on the failure path as well, and unregister after each test. Identifying only that something is registered and not unregistered, without the missing decrement, scores at most half. Attributing the timeouts to emulator speed, network slowness or flake scores zero.

Adding `@FixMethodOrder`, an ordering rule, or renaming methods to obtain the order that happens to be green scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require saying why it does not hold: the 8th and the extra single-class run show the boundary moving with the position of `updatesQuantityInPlace`, so a fixed order would hide the leak behind whichever arrangement currently works and would break again the moment a test is added.

No timeout policy is raised, no `Thread.sleep` and no polling loop is introduced. Any of those scores zero. Full marks require stating why a longer timeout cannot work here: the counter never returns to zero, so the wait has no length at which it succeeds - it only makes the run longer.

Tomas's theory is addressed explicitly - the preference is real shared state and worth cleaning up, but it cannot produce an idle-resource timeout in classes that never read it, and the failures name a resource `AccountTest` does not use. Silently ignoring the theory scores at most half. Adopting it as the cause of the nineteen failures scores zero.
All twenty-three `@Test` methods remain and no assertion is changed, deleted or weakened. Removing or merging tests, or relaxing an assertion to get a green run, scores zero.

`docs/nightly-isolation.md` exists and gives a separate verdict on each of the three proposals. A document that answers only the technical question without addressing the proposals scores at most half.

# One orders test fails in a third of a second and the other sits there for twenty-six, both since we deleted the last AsyncTask

## Problem Description

`com.northwind.orders`, Android, Kotlin. `OrdersListTest` had been green for
about two years. On 28 August we finished moving the last of our networking off
`AsyncTask` onto Retrofit and OkHttp, and the same commit added the little status
chip that ticks on the order detail screen. Nothing about the layouts changed -
same ids, same view types, same strings - and from that build on two of the three
tests have been red.

They are red in two different ways and I think that matters, but nobody here has
been able to say why.

`loadsOrdersForReturningCustomer` blows up in under half a second with nothing
in the hierarchy. `showsRefundBadgeOnRefundedOrder` does not blow up at all; it
sits for twenty-six seconds and then throws something about idle conditions. The
third test still passes and I would like it to stay that way.

Priya spent last week on it. She followed a blog post and added a
`NetworkIdlingResource`, wired it up, and it made no difference at all - the same
test still fails instantly and the same test still hangs. Her proposal this
morning is to delete her class and put `Thread.sleep(3000)` in front of each
assertion, on the grounds that this is what we had before 2019, it was green for
years, three seconds is longer than any call we make, and she has spent long
enough on it. Karim's counter-proposal is to keep the class and raise the idle
timeout to ninety seconds so at least the slow one gets a chance to finish.

I do not think either of them is right and I cannot articulate why. Sprint review
is Thursday.

Attached: the test class, Priya's class, the repository, the ticker and the
detail activity, the module build file, a summary of what the migration changed,
and the instrumentation output from before it, after it, and after Priya's fix,
with the logcat from the hanging test and the gateway timings.

## Output Specification

1. Get all three tests in `OrdersListTest` reporting correctly. Do not delete or
   weaken an assertion, and do not remove a test.
2. You may change production code under `app/src/main/`.
3. Write `docs/orders-async-fix.md` for a reviewer who has never read this
   framework's documentation: why each of the two failures has the cause it has,
   why they are not the same problem, and what you did with each of the two
   proposals on the table.
evals.expected_output:
1. Get all three tests in `OrdersListTest` reporting correctly. Do not delete or
   weaken an assertion, and do not remove a test.
2. You may change production code under `app/src/main/`.
3. Write `docs/orders-async-fix.md` for a reviewer who has never read this
   framework's documentation: why each of the two failures has the cause it has,
   why they are not the same problem, and what you did with each of the two
   proposals on the table.
assertions: Giving the two failures the same cause, or wrapping the ticker in an idling resource, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the diagnosis and the repair: `OrderStatusTicker` reposts itself to the main handler with no delay, so the main message queue is never empty of work that is due now and the framework's first synchronisation condition can never be met - which is why the exception names the looper and not a resource - and the ticker is fixed so it runs on the cadence the migration note describes rather than continuously. Naming the ticker as the cause but leaving it reposting immediately scores at most half.

Full marks require all three: the test registers the same instance `OrdersRepository` increments rather than constructing its own, both `onFailure` branches decrement so the 404 on `GET /v1/orders/NW-10091` cannot strand the counter, and the resource is unregistered after each test. Leaving `setUp` constructing and registering a fresh `NetworkIdlingResource()` scores zero. Correcting the instance without the failure-path decrements scores at most half, since that change turns a resource that never blocked into one that blocks forever on the seeded 404.

No `Thread.sleep`, no polling or retry loop, and no change to the idling timeout policy anywhere in the delivered code. Any of those scores zero, including a sleep kept only in the test that hangs, and including a shorter sleep than the three seconds proposed.

`docs/orders-async-fix.md` tells a reviewer why the old code was green without any of this - the framework waited on the message queue and on the task type the migration deleted - and why one of the two remaining failures is a gap in what it can see while the other is the opposite, work it can see and that never ends. An explanation that says only 'the framework needs help with background work' scores at most half. An explanation that attributes the hang to emulator slowness or network latency scores zero.

Priya's sleep and Karim's ninety-second timeout each get an explicit verdict with the reason it does not hold for these particular failures. Addressing only one, or rejecting both without reference to what the evidence shows, scores at most half.

`showsEmptyStateForNewAccount` is not modified and still passes, and no assertion in the class is deleted, relaxed or replaced with a presence check. Any change to the passing test, or any weakened assertion, scores zero.
`docs/orders-async-fix.md` exists and addresses the two failures separately. A single combined explanation scores at most half.

# Five automation requests from product and I need a verdict on each before Thursday

## Problem Description

`com.northwind.shop`, Android, Kotlin. After the August release went badly Dana
in product wrote down five things she wants covered automatically and put them
on Thursday's planning agenda. Bilal, who joined us in July, took a run at all
five last week and got a long way on one of them and nowhere on the rest. His
notes are attached, along with Dana's list.

The two loudest opinions in the room are both absolute and I do not believe
either one.

Dana's position is that the app is ours, so all five are automatable and the only
question is how long each takes. Hendrik's position is that anything the user can
see which is not one of our own screens is out of scope for this job, and that we
should cut 1, 3 and 4 on that basis and stop discussing it.

What I actually need is a per-request answer I can defend at planning: for each
of the five, whether we cover it here, cover part of it here, or do not cover it
here - and for the parts we are not covering, what the honest alternative is, so
Dana does not leave the room thinking the gap has been filled when it has not.

Where something is coverable, I would rather see the test than a description of
it. Our conventions are in the one class we already have; follow them.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/automation-verdicts.md` with a numbered section per request. Each
   section gives one of three verdicts - covered here, covered in part here, or
   not covered here - and for anything partial or refused, states plainly what
   is being given up and what would cover it instead.
2. For every request you say is covered in whole or in part, add the test under
   `app/src/androidTest/java/com/northwind/shop/` and list any module build file
   change it needs.
3. Do not change the existing method in `OrderHistoryTest.kt`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/automation-verdicts.md` with a numbered section per request. Each
   section gives one of three verdicts - covered here, covered in part here, or
   not covered here - and for anything partial or refused, states plainly what
   is being given up and what would cover it instead.
2. For every request you say is covered in whole or in part, add the test under
   `app/src/androidTest/java/com/northwind/shop/` and list any module build file
   change it needs.
3. Do not change the existing method in `OrderHistoryTest.kt`.
assertions: Full marks require citing the manifest's `android:process=":sync"` declarations and the two pids in Bilal's logcat, saying that a test running in the shop's process cannot match views owned by another process no matter that the code is ours, and naming the framework's own multi-process facility as what closes the gap rather than an ordinary test or a general-purpose cross-app driver. Treating it as a normal in-app screen that Bilal simply matched wrongly scores zero. Refusing it as 'another app' or handing it wholesale to a cross-app driver on Hendrik's reasoning also scores zero.

The picker's own screen is declared out of reach from here, and the part Dana actually lost twice this year - the returned image not appearing on the profile - is covered in-process by stubbing the activity result and driving `ProfileAvatar.onAvatarPicked` through the app's own path, with the module build file gaining what stubbing needs. Accepting the whole request, or refusing the whole request, scores zero. Splitting it without delivering the in-app test scores at most half.

No delivered test or proposed step matches against the phone's settings screen or the picker's screen with in-process view matchers, and the verdicts do not imply that a longer wait or a better matcher would have made Bilal's attempts work. Any test that does so scores zero here, as does an answer that explains his failures on those two as a matcher problem.

The answer explains how the screenshot and the `NoMatchingViewException` are both true - the message is not drawn in the activity's own window, which is what a plain assertion looks in - and covers it either by targeting that separate window explicitly or by asserting the in-app consequence instead, with the trade-off stated. Delivering `onView(withText("Saved to your wishlist")).check(matches(isDisplayed()))` with no window handling scores zero. Declaring the request uncoverable scores at most half.

The trip through the phone's settings screen is out; the banner's behaviour once the permission state changes is in, covered by putting the app into each permission state from the test harness rather than by navigating to it. Dropping the whole request scores zero. Keeping the whole request scores zero.

Each delivered `@Test` method has a single assertion target and covers one numbered request. A single method that chains two or more of the five, or a method that ends in a run of unrelated assertions, scores zero for this criterion.

The determinate one: a test that brings position 213 of a four-hundred-row list into view before asserting on it, with the list package added to the module build file, plus an explanation of why Bilal's dump held only nine rows. Refusing or deferring this request scores zero. Asserting without first bringing the row into view scores at most half.
`docs/automation-verdicts.md` exists with a numbered section and one of the three verdicts for each of the five requests. Any request left without an explicit verdict scores at most half.
